title: MIND: Monge Inception Distance for Generative Models Evaluation
claim: A cheaper metric with far fewer samples tracks training progress as well as or better than the standard expensive benchmark.
layout: 2 panels, left curves then right heatmap, shared metric legend
description: Two panels side by side. The left panel is a line plot of metric value against training step (0 to 3e6) on a log y-axis, with a dashed grid. Five curves are shown. A grey FID with 50k samples and a light grey FID with 5k samples are drawn alongside three red curves for MIND with 1k, 2k and 5k samples, going from light to dark red. All curves drop sharply and then flatten. MIND at 5k closely follows the FID 50k curve but with a wider range, while the smaller-sample curves sit higher. The right panel is an 8x8 green correlation heatmap, annotated with numbers, comparing negative step, FID at 5k, 10k, 25k and 50k, and MIND at 1k, 2k and 5k. A colorbar runs from 0.80 to 1.00. MIND rows have the highest correlation with step and with FID 50k.
caption: (Left) MIND metric during a diffusion model training run on ImageNet-64 (log scale), illustrating how $\MIND_{5k}$ can be used to replace $\FID_{50k}$, with a larger range - see Section [ref]. (Right) Correlation with number of training steps - better for $\MIND_{1k}$ and $\MIND_{5k}$ than FID with $50$k samples.
abstract: We propose the Monge Inception Distance (MIND), a metric for evaluating generative models that addresses key limitations of the widely adopted FrÃ©chet Inception Distance (FID). The MIND metric leverages the sliced Wasserstein distance to compare distributions by averaging one-dimensional optimal transport distances, efficiently computed via sorting. This approach circumvents the estimation of high-dimensional means and covariance matrices, which underlie FID's poor sample complexity and vulnerability to adversarial attacks. We empirically demonstrate three primary advantages: (i) it is more sample-efficient by one order of magnitude, (ii) it is faster to compute by two orders of magnitude, (iii) it is more robust to adversarial attacks such as moment-matching. We show that MIND with 5k samples can replace the evaluation performance of FID with 50k samples, providing high correlation with this standard benchmark and superior discriminative performance. We further demonstrate that even smaller sample sizes (e.g., 1k or 2k) remain highly informative for rapid model iteration.
